title: Severe vomiting in early pregnancy — recognise, investigate and act safely

blocks.text: Severe vomiting in early pregnancy — recognise, investigate and act safely

AMaC MRCP PACES23 | Round 5 | R5-239 | Station 2: acute consultation | 20 minutes | Communication, clinical judgement and patient welfare (C, E, F, G) | AMaC educational scoring, not official PACES marks
A patient at nine weeks of pregnancy has persistent vomiting, weight loss and cannot retain food or fluids. Take a focused history, determine urgency and explain your plan to the patient.

sections.heading: 4. The Hook and the Examiner Trap

blocks.text: Hook: Hyperemesis gravidarum is possible when nausea and vomiting cause major functional impairment. Ketonuria is not a measure of dehydration or disease severity and must not guide admission alone. Trap: Avoid older teaching that urine ketones quantify dehydration; consider competing causes and antiemetic adverse effects.

rows: “First, I want to check how unwell you are.”
Assess stability and the specific emergency signs.
“I’ll ask questions that help us distinguish the causes.”

Use PUQE or another validated symptom index, assess weight change, intake, orthostatic symptoms, urine output, abdominal pain, bleeding, infection and alternative causes. Check electrolytes and renal function.
“I will arrange tests and support appropriate to the risk.”

Assess need for ambulatory or inpatient care, IV normal saline with potassium if appropriate to monitored electrolytes, pregnancy-safe antiemetics following stepwise guidance; give thiamine to patients admitted with vomiting or severely reduced intake, especially before dextrose.
“I will explain when we must act urgently.”

Inability to retain fluids, haemodynamic instability, marked electrolyte disturbance or neurological signs warrants urgent hospital assessment. Review VTE risk and give prophylaxis to hospitalised patients when appropriate.
Introduces self, validates concerns and agrees to assess.

Checks the most important competing cause and severity discriminator.
States a diagnosis as proven without evidence.

Use PUQE or HELP and clinical assessment of oral intake, weight loss, hydration, function, electrolytes and alternate diagnoses; ketonuria must not be used as a severity marker. Treat with appropriate pregnancy antiemetics, isotonic saline and guided potassium replacement if required; give thiamine to admitted patients with prolonged vomiting or poor intake, especially before dextrose.

States rationale, checks contraindications and escalation context; Danger: delaying treatment because ketones are absent, or administering dextrose before thiamine in a nutritionally depleted patient.

blocks.text: Patient is concerned about the symptoms and asks: ““Are medicines safe for my baby?”” The role-player provides symptoms from the brief and relevant positive/negative history only when asked; avoid volunteering the diagnosis. Respond to clear empathetic explanations.

Release if asked: Use PUQE or another validated symptom index, assess weight change, intake, orthostatic symptoms, urine output, abdominal pain, bleeding, infection and alternative causes. Check electrolytes and renal function.

EXAMINER: What is the most likely syndrome?
MODEL (corrected critical decision): Use PUQE or HELP and clinical assessment of oral intake, weight loss, hydration, function, electrolytes and alternate diagnoses; ketonuria must not be used as a severity marker. Treat with appropriate pregnancy antiemetics, isotonic saline and guided potassium replacement if required; give thiamine to admitted patients with prolonged vomiting or poor intake, especially before dextrose.

EXAMINER: What separates this from major alternatives?  MODEL: Use PUQE or another validated symptom index, assess weight change, intake, orthostatic symptoms, urine output, abdominal pain, bleeding, infection and alternative causes. Check electrolytes and renal function.

EXAMINER: What would you do first?  MODEL: Assess need for ambulatory or inpatient care, IV normal saline with potassium if appropriate to monitored electrolytes, pregnancy-safe antiemetics following stepwise guidance; give thiamine to patients admitted with vomiting or severely reduced intake, especially before dextrose.

EXAMINER: What finding changes urgency?  MODEL: Inability to retain fluids, haemodynamic instability, marked electrolyte disturbance or neurological signs warrants urgent hospital assessment. Review VTE risk and give prophylaxis to hospitalised patients when appropriate.

EXAMINER: How would you answer the patient?  MODEL: “Some anti-sickness medicines have reassuring pregnancy safety data. We can discuss the options and balance small potential risks against the harm from uncontrolled vomiting.”
Curveball: the patient becomes acutely more unwell. Candidate should stop the routine consultation, reassess ABCDE, summon appropriate help and act on the case-specific danger.
• [R1 · C/G] Introduces self, validates concerns and agrees to assess.
• [R2 · C/E] Elicits targeted history and red-flag assessment.
• [R3 · E] Gives a defensible working diagnosis.
• [R4 · E] Identifies the correct core tests and pathway.
• [R5 · E/G] Names a specific trigger and urgent escalation.
• [R6 · F/G] Explains risks, plan and next steps clearly.

FAIL — PATIENT: “I am worried.” CANDIDATE: “It is probably fine.” [R1 Fail; R6 Fail] EXAMINER: “What are the important tests?” CANDIDATE: “Maybe some routine bloods.” [R2–R4 Fail] EXAMINER: “Can this deteriorate?” CANDIDATE: “Not likely.” [R5 Fail] Examiner note: unsafe minimisation and absent decision-making.

PASS — CANDIDATE: “I’m sorry you are feeling unwell; may I ask a few questions and examine you?” [R1 Pass] PATIENT: “Yes.” CANDIDATE: “Use PUQE or another validated symptom index, assess weight change, intake, orthostatic symptoms, urine output, abdominal pain, bleeding, infection and alternative causes. Check electrolytes and renal function.” [R2 Pass] EXAMINER: “What do you think?” CANDIDATE: “Hyperemesis gravidarum is possible when nausea and vomiting cause major functional impairment. Ketonuria is not a measure of dehydration or disease severity and must not guide admission alone.” [R3 Pass] EXAMINER: “Next steps?” CANDIDATE: “Assess need for ambulatory or inpatient care, IV normal saline with potassium if appropriate to monitored electrolytes, pregnancy-safe antiemetics following stepwise guidance; give thiamine to patients admitted with vomiting or severely reduced intake, especially before dextrose.” [R4 Pass] CANDIDATE: “I also need to act if Inability to retain fluids, haemodynamic instability, marked electrolyte disturbance or neurological signs warrants urgent hospital assessment. Review VTE risk and give prophylaxis to hospitalised patients when appropriate.” [R5 Pass] PATIENT: ““Are medicines safe for my baby?”” CANDIDATE: ““Some anti-sickness medicines have reassuring pregnancy safety data. We can discuss the options and balance small potential risks against the harm from uncontrolled vomiting.”” [R6 Pass] Examiner note: essential assessment, disposition and communication.

HIGH-PERFORMANCE — CANDIDATE: “I can see that this is worrying. I will check immediately for signs that would change how urgently we need to act.” [R1 High-performance] EXAMINER: “How will you separate the diagnoses?” CANDIDATE: “Use PUQE or another validated symptom index, assess weight change, intake, orthostatic symptoms, urine output, abdominal pain, bleeding, infection and alternative causes. Check electrolytes and renal function. I would also verify the relevant negatives, not assume they are absent.” [R2 High-performance] EXAMINER: “Your interpretation?” CANDIDATE: “Hyperemesis gravidarum is possible when nausea and vomiting cause major functional impairment. Ketonuria is not a measure of dehydration or disease severity and must not guide admission alone. But Avoid older teaching that urine ketones quantify dehydration; consider competing causes and antiemetic adverse effects.” [R3 High-performance] EXAMINER: “Prioritise management.” CANDIDATE: “Assess need for ambulatory or inpatient care, IV normal saline with potassium if appropriate to monitored electrolytes, pregnancy-safe antiemetics following stepwise guidance; give thiamine to patients admitted with vomiting or severely reduced intake, especially before dextrose.” [R4 High-performance] EXAMINER: “And the emergency?” CANDIDATE: “Inability to retain fluids, haemodynamic instability, marked electrolyte disturbance or neurological signs warrants urgent hospital assessment. Review VTE risk and give prophylaxis to hospitalised patients when appropriate. I would reassess immediately if the clinical state changed.” [R5 High-performance] PATIENT: ““Are medicines safe for my baby?”” CANDIDATE: ““Some anti-sickness medicines have reassuring pregnancy safety data. We can discuss the options and balance small potential risks against the harm from uncontrolled vomiting.” Could you tell me what you have understood and what worries you most?” [R6 High-performance] Examiner note: discriminating reasoning and specific anticipation of harm.

R2/R3: Uncritical diagnosis without evaluating: Use PUQE or another validated symptom index, assess weight change, intake, orthostatic symptoms, urine output, abdominal pain, bleeding, infection and alternative causes. Check electrolytes and renal function.

R4: Unprioritised actions rather than: Assess need for ambulatory or inpatient care, IV normal saline with potassium if appropriate to monitored electrolytes, pregnancy-safe antiemetics following stepwise guidance; give thiamine to patients admitted with vomiting or severely reduced intake, especially before dextrose.

R5: Misses: Inability to retain fluids, haemodynamic instability, marked electrolyte disturbance or neurological signs warrants urgent hospital assessment. Review VTE risk and give prophylaxis to hospitalised patients when appropriate.
R6: Fails to address the patient’s actual concern.
“Let me check for deterioration before continuing.”
“I should not assume a diagnosis is proven without the discriminating findings.”

“The urgent threshold here is: Inability to retain fluids, haemodynamic instability, marked electrolyte disturbance or neurological signs warrants urgent hospital assessment. Review VTE risk and give prophylaxis to hospitalised patients when appropriate.”

Clinical correction,— Use PUQE or HELP and clinical assessment of oral intake, weight loss, hydration, function, electrolytes and alternate diagnoses; ketonuria must not be used as a severity marker. Treat with appropriate pregnancy antiemetics, isotonic saline and guided potassium replacement if required; give thiamine to admitted patients with prolonged vomiting or poor intake, especially before dextrose.

THINK: Hyperemesis gravidarum is possible when nausea and vomiting cause major functional impairment. Ketonuria is not a measure of dehydration or disease severity and must not guide admission alone. SAY: avoid certainty without confirmation. DO: Assess need for ambulatory or inpatient care, IV normal saline with potassium if appropriate to monitored electrolytes, pregnancy-safe antiemetics following stepwise guidance; give thiamine to patients admitted with vomiting or severely reduced intake, especially before dextrose. NUMBERS: 20-minute encounter. TRAP: Avoid older teaching that urine ketones quantify dehydration; consider competing causes and antiemetic adverse effects. FINISH: Inability to retain fluids, haemodynamic instability, marked electrolyte disturbance or neurological signs warrants urgent hospital assessment. Review VTE risk and give prophylaxis to hospitalised patients when appropriate.
